content: 1. Patients receiving rifampicin and opiate users undergoing methadone substitution therapy require careful consideration due to potential drug interactions and adherence challenges. 2. The widespread use of rifampicin-containing fixed-dose combinations for treating drug-susceptible tuberculosis (TB) has led to a decreased demand for single-dose rifampicin by TB programs. 3. Quality-assured supplies of rifampicin should be utilized to ensure efficacy and safety. 4. Primary care facilities and HIV programs should implement stepwise guidance to maximize the effectiveness of rifampicin and prevent its misuse as a broad-spectrum antibiotic in the community. 5. Fixed-dose combinations of rifampicin and isoniazid, including dispersible formulations for children, should be used whenever possible to reduce the pill burden for patients. 6. Combinations of 300 mg isoniazid with 300 mg rifapentine are now available, facilitating the administration of the 3HP regimen for adults. 7. For children, dispersible formulations of both isoniazid and rifapentine can simplify the administration of the 3HP regimen, which is more likely to be completed due to its shorter duration. 8. Concerns about adherence should not prevent the initiation of TB preventive treatment (TPT). Support should be provided to ensure better person-centered care. 9. There are no evidence-based recommendations on managing interruptions in TPT, such as how many missed doses can be compensated for by extending treatment without compromising efficacy. 10. Individuals at risk of peripheral neuropathy, such as those with malnutrition, chronic alcohol dependence, HIV infection, renal failure, diabetes, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, should receive pyridoxine (vitamin B6) when taking isoniazid-containing regimens. 11. In populations with a high prevalence of slow acetylators, a different dose of isoniazid may be required to avoid toxicity. 12. Combination tablets of co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, and pyridoxine could be provided to people with HIV. The unavailability of pyridoxine should not be a reason to withhold TPT. 13. Interventions to enhance adherence and completion of treatment should be tailored to each risk group and local context. 14. In areas with high background resistance to rifampicin, such as Eastern Europe, it is crucial to test the strain from the presumed source for drug susceptibility to improve the likelihood of TPT success. 15. Contacts of patients with laboratory-confirmed isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible TB may be offered a 4-month regimen of daily rifampicin. 16. If rifampicin monoresistance or other contraindications to rifampicin exist, a regimen of isoniazid for six months or longer may be the most appropriate option. 17. In many settings, rifampicin resistance is often accompanied by isoniazid resistance (MDR-TB), necessitating the use of other drugs. 18. For contacts exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB, six months of daily levofloxacin should be used as TPT. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate certainty of evidence. 19. Drug-resistant TB is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality from antimicrobial-resistant organisms, making it essential to take all measures to reduce the risk of secondary cases of MDR/RR-TB, including the use of effective TPT regimens. 20. Levofloxacin is the preferred fluoroquinolone for TPT and has been shown to be generally safe, with mild or moderate adverse events reported in children but no serious adverse events. 21. Levofloxacin can be used in children and adolescents, with better completion and tolerability observed in younger populations compared to older ones. 22. There is no requirement to test for TB infection before starting levofloxacin in children who are contacts of people with MDR/RR-TB. 23. Although concerns about fluoroquinolone use in children exist due to cartilage development issues observed in animal studies, similar effects have not been found in humans. 24. TPT with levofloxacin during pregnancy requires a risk-benefit assessment and an informed choice by the pregnant woman on whether to take TPT or defer it until after pregnancy. 25. Pregnancy increases the risk of progression from TB infection to disease and poor maternal and fetal outcomes if TB disease occurs. 26. MDR/RR-TB in pregnancy is a serious condition, and some drugs used to treat MDR-TB may be toxic to the fetus. 27. Levofloxacin concentrations in breast milk are much lower than the dose for infants and are not expected to cause adverse effects in breastfed infants. Its use should not be suspended during breastfeeding. 28. While fluoroquinolone effects on bone and cartilage observed in animals have not been seen in humans, data and follow-up times for infants are limited. 29. Recent alerts have highlighted safety concerns associated with prolonged fluoroquinolone use in humans. 30. Levofloxacin can be used in people with HIV, with no specific drug-drug interactions observed with antiretroviral therapy. 31. Levofloxacin should not be given to individuals allergic to fluoroquinolones or those with contraindications to this drug class. It should be discontinued if serious adverse reactions occur. 32. Health programs and clinicians should ensure eligibility for levofloxacin use, maximize treatment completion, and follow up with contacts regardless of whether TPT was completed. 33. Contacts of people with rifampicin-resistant TB are usually treated as for MDR-TB unless susceptibility to isoniazid is reliably confirmed, in which case isoniazid may be considered an effective TPT option. 34. Levofloxacin is widely available as a generic drug in both adult and pediatric formulations. 35. The six-month duration of levofloxacin treatment may seem long compared to shorter TPT regimens for drug-susceptible TB, but it remains the preferred option for MDR/RR-TB prevention. 36. People receiving TPT should be provided with advice on managing adverse events and treatment. 37. Drug-susceptibility testing of the source case strain provides important additional information, especially in settings with high fluoroquinolone resistance. 38. Screening all household and close contacts for co-prevalent TB disease is essential. 39. The capacity of a program to provide TPT for MDR/RR-TB should be carefully planned to ensure all necessary resources are in place, including the ability to rule out TB disease, perform quality-assured drug susceptibility testing, deliver medications, and monitor adverse events. 40. Stakeholder engagement in the community is important to address constraints to implementation. 41. A pediatric formulation of levofloxacin can be used, with dosage instructions provided in the WHO operational handbook on TPT. 42. While ethambutol is considered safe in pregnancy, ethionamide has been associated with teratogenic potential at high doses in animal studies, with minimal data available on human pregnancy. 43. There is limited evidence for the optimal duration of MDR-TB preventive treatment, which should be based on clinical judgment. Levofloxacin has been given for six, nine, or twelve months in studies conducted so far. 44. Monitoring and evaluation systems should include coverage of TPT with levofloxacin among contacts exposed to MDR/RR-TB, with appropriate recording and reporting tools available. 45. Electronic case-based monitoring can facilitate TPT implementation, and standardized indicators should be measured regularly to inform decision-makers.
